lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on urban water management.
lecture.script: When rain falls on a paved schoolyard, it travels rapidly into drains. One school replaced a strip of paving with a shallow garden. During storms, water pooled among the plants and then entered the soil gradually. The garden did not reduce the amount of rain that fell. Its benefit was to delay the arrival of water at the drains, especially during the heaviest minutes of a storm.

questions.prompt: What benefit of the garden does the lecturer emphasize?
options: It reduced the amount of rain falling nearby.
It slowed the flow of rainwater into drains.
It diverted water from the garden onto the paving.
It made the soil dry rapidly after storms.

explanation.correct: The garden held rainwater temporarily, delaying its arrival at drains.

distractors.0: The lecturer explicitly says the project did not change rainfall.
distractors.2: Water flowed toward the planted strip rather than away from it.
distractors.3: Water entered the soil gradually, and fast drying is not described as a goal.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on musical manuscript collections.
lecture.script: Before mechanical recording, families preserved songs by writing down the words and sometimes the melody. A local archive has three manuscripts of the same song, all copied within twenty years. The tune is almost identical in all three, but one manuscript ends with a different verse. At first, the editors planned to treat that verse as a copying error. They changed their minds when they found a letter in which the copyist described hearing the verse at a wedding. The letter does not prove which version is oldest. It does show that someone sang the uncommon verse in a particular setting. The printed edition therefore includes all three texts. Readers can see how the differences circulated without assuming that any surviving copy is necessarily the original.

questions.prompt: What made the editors reconsider their interpretation of the unusual verse?
options: An older manuscript with the same verse.
A note in the manuscript correcting the tune.
A recording of its copyist singing the verse.
A letter about a performance of it at a wedding.

explanation.correct: The wedding account showed the verse was performed, so it need not have been accidental.

distractors.0: No older manuscript with the verse was discovered.
distractors.1: The tunes are similar, and the new evidence was a separate letter.
distractors.2: The examples are from before mechanical recording and no recording is mentioned.

questions.prompt: What does the lecturer say the letter leaves unresolved?
options: Where the unusual verse was heard.
Who wrote down the unusual verse.
Which version came first.
Whether the printed edition includes that verse.

explanation.correct: The letter documents one performance but cannot establish priority.

distractors.0: The setting was a wedding.
distractors.1: The letter was written by the copyist whose manuscript contained the verse.
distractors.3: The edition contains all three versions.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on daytime animal surveys.
lecture.script: Suppose you want to compare the number of butterflies in two fields. You walk a fixed route at noon and record every butterfly you notice. The first field is open to the sun, while the second is shaded by trees. You see twice as many butterflies in the open field. Is the population there twice as large? Possibly, but your count does not establish that. Butterflies are more likely to fly at higher temperatures, and a flying insect is easier to see than one resting under a leaf. Repeating the walk at noon for a week would help if the first day were unusual. It would not remove the difference in visibility if the shaded field remained cooler on every visit. To investigate that problem, a team could record the temperature and visit each field under several comparable temperature conditions. The resulting counts would still depend on how well observers detect butterflies. But they would give researchers a better basis for deciding whether the initial gap reflects a population difference or simply a difference in activity at the time of observation.

questions.prompt: Why might the initial count exaggerate a difference between the two populations?
options: Butterflies in the warmer field may be easier to see.
The route through the warmer field may be longer.
The shaded field may attract more visiting observers.
Butterflies in both fields may leave at noon.

explanation.correct: Butterflies are more active in warmth, making more of them visible in the open field.

distractors.1: The lecturer presents a fixed route and focuses on visibility.
distractors.2: The number of observers is not the explanation under discussion.
distractors.3: No midday departure is presented; the issue is flight activity and detection.

questions.prompt: What limitation remains if both fields are surveyed at noon every day?
options: An unusual first day necessarily determines the final results.
The survey design makes it impossible to measure field temperatures.
The same temperature difference can persist.
The observer cannot use a consistent walking route.

explanation.correct: Repeating the timing can preserve the systematic shade and temperature difference.

distractors.0: Additional visits make the study less dependent on any one unusual day.
distractors.1: Measuring temperature is a proposed improvement.
distractors.3: The lecturer begins with a fixed walking route, which can be repeated.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on furniture conservation.
lecture.script: One antique chair in our collection has a faded rectangular patch on its seat. That looks like damage, but the museum will keep it. The patch shows where a cushion protected the material while the exposed fabric changed color. A new covering would make the seat look more uniform. It would also hide evidence of how the chair was used before it reached the museum.

questions.prompt: Why do the conservators keep the faded area visible?
options: The contrast provides information about past use.
Replacing the fabric would make it fade faster.
The protected area shows where new fabric was added.
The seat would look less uniform if restored.

explanation.correct: The differing colors indicate where a cushion once protected the seat.

distractors.1: The talk makes no claim about how quickly replacement material would fade.
distractors.2: The patch came from uneven exposure of existing fabric.
distractors.3: The lecturer says replacement would make the surface more uniform.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on teaching with historical maps.
lecture.script: A reproduction enables students to examine a large historical map without exposing fragile paper to repeated handling. But a reproduction can unintentionally change what students notice. In one workshop, we showed half the class an old route map as a high-resolution scan. Other students saw a print in its original dimensions, slightly larger than a notebook. The first group enlarged the settlement names and discussed spelling. The second group commented more often on how several routes surrounded one large blank area. Neither group was mistaken. A scan makes close inspection convenient, while a print of the whole sheet makes the relative positions easier to take in at once. The instructor now supplies both views, with separate questions tailored to the kinds of observation each supports.

questions.prompt: Why does the instructor now provide both views of the map?
options: Neither view alone shows the complete route map.
The print is needed to correct errors introduced by scanning.
Students can use the scan to identify damage to the original.
Each view makes a different feature easier to study.

explanation.correct: One view facilitates magnifying names, and the other makes overall spatial relationships easier to see.

distractors.0: The difference is in how students inspect the map, not missing content.
distractors.1: The discussion concerns attention and scale rather than inaccuracies in digitization.
distractors.2: Protecting original paper is mentioned, but identifying damage is not the workshop goal.

questions.prompt: Which observation was reported more often by students who saw the original-size print?
options: Some names used unusual spellings.
Several lines enclosed a relatively empty region.
The page had already been damaged by handling.
The print reproduced fewer names than the scan.

explanation.correct: The print group more often noticed routes enclosing a blank area.

distractors.0: The scan group discussed the spelling of names.
distractors.2: No observation of original damage was reported.
distractors.3: The two presentation formats emphasize different features, not different sets of names.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on pedestrian wayfinding.
lecture.script: In a railway terminal, signs are often placed where a designer sees a long, uninterrupted line of sight on a plan. Passengers do not look at the plan. They read signs while pulling luggage, checking a ticket, or following a crowd. A station tested two designs for signs directing passengers to its exit. The first put large lettering near the entrance to the main hall. The second repeated a smaller arrow just before each point where someone had to turn. People using the first design took less time to find the sign. However, more of them made a wrong turn afterward. The station might have chosen the larger sign if its only measure had been how quickly test participants first looked up. Instead, the researchers accompanied each participant until that person reached the street. They chose the repeated arrows because the goal was successful navigation. This example does not establish that smaller lettering is generally better. A sign can fail because travelers cannot read it, but it can also fail because the instruction arrives too early to help them make the decision it describes.

questions.prompt: Why did the station choose the design with repeated arrows?
options: Its first arrow was identified sooner.
It helped more passengers avoid wrong turns.
Its lettering could be read from a greater distance.
It better matched the designers’ terminal plan.

explanation.correct: The station used successful navigation as its criterion, and wrong turns were less common with repeated arrows.

distractors.0: Passengers found the larger initial sign sooner.
distractors.2: The arrows had smaller lettering and their range was not the deciding factor.
distractors.3: The test followed what passengers actually did rather than comparing designs on a plan.

questions.prompt: What distinction does the example illustrate?
options: Passengers who read tickets move more slowly than those who follow others.
Terminal exits require clearer designs than railway platforms.
Reading a station plan is easier than reading a sign.
Noticing an instruction and acting on it accurately are different outcomes.

explanation.correct: The first sign drew attention quickly but did not guide passengers as successfully to the street.

distractors.0: Those activities are examples of divided attention, with no measured comparison.
distractors.1: No comparison with signs for platforms is provided.
distractors.2: Plans describe the designers' point of view; relative reading difficulty was not measured.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on seeds kept in collections.
lecture.script: A seed bank keeps plants available for future research by drying and cooling their seeds. But counting envelopes tells you little about whether the collection is still useful. At intervals, staff take a few seeds from each batch and try to grow them. A sample that once sprouted readily may perform poorly years later, even when the envelope and the seeds inside look unchanged.

questions.prompt: Why do staff try to grow some stored seeds?
options: To find out which envelopes were opened before.
To compare the appearance of seeds from different plants.
To determine whether seeds in the batch remain viable.
To develop a new method of cooling stored material.

explanation.correct: The test checks an ability that cannot always be inferred from appearance.

distractors.0: The checks address whether seeds sprout rather than whether their envelopes were opened.
distractors.1: Appearance can remain the same even as germination declines.
distractors.3: Cooling is a storage practice, not the purpose of these trials.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on naming features on maps.
lecture.script: An archive recently digitized street plans produced during a period when the city often renamed streets. The archive team considered searchable text a priority, but it faced a problem. A reader who knows a modern name might never find a plan labeled with an earlier name. Automatically replacing every old name with the current one would make the plans easier to search, but it would also hide part of what the documents record. The team kept the names exactly as they appear and added searchable links to modern equivalents when a match could be confirmed. Some names are still unresolved. The website marks uncertain identifications explicitly rather than guessing. Users can therefore distinguish between original wording, a confirmed cross-reference, and a possible match.

questions.prompt: How did the archive help readers search using a newer name?
options: It added links when the old and new names could be matched.
It replaced obsolete labels before scanning each plan.
It removed plans that contained unidentified street names.
It allowed users to rename streets in the archive.

explanation.correct: Confirmed links help users locate plans while retaining their original wording.

distractors.1: The original labels were kept as evidence.
distractors.2: Uncertain identifications are marked, not discarded.
distractors.3: The solution is editorial cross-referencing, not user editing.

questions.prompt: Why did the team refuse to replace historical labels automatically?
options: The newer names are generally harder to search.
The old names were less likely to refer to more than one street.
Their wording is part of the information the plans preserve.
The scanned labels could not be read by most visitors.

explanation.correct: Replacing labels would preserve geography but hide a historical record of naming.

distractors.0: Modern names are precisely what some readers know.
distractors.1: The lecture does not compare ambiguity in the two naming systems.
distractors.3: Legibility was not the reason for preserving original names.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on the design of playgrounds.
lecture.script: Public parks often contain seats at the edge of a playground. A landscape architect wanted to understand why some benches were occupied even on quiet mornings, while others were rarely used. Three benches had the best views of the entire play area, and she expected them to be the most popular. Instead, the busiest bench faced only one corner of the playground. When asked about their choice, caregivers said that the path behind this bench let them stand up, walk around it, and reach the playground quickly. People sitting in the benches with better views had to follow a longer path around a fence. The architect had assumed a bench was a stationary viewing point. Her visitors treated it as part of a short route. The study did not show that sightlines were unimportant; caregivers rejected places from which they could not see the equipment at all. It suggested that a design should consider visibility together with the speed of access. The architect later tested layouts in which benches had useful views and more than one way to reach the children.

questions.prompt: Why was the bench facing a single corner widely used?
options: Its position made it quick to reach the children.
The other benches gave a poorer view of the equipment.
It was easier to find from outside the park.
Its users could sit farther from the playground.

explanation.correct: The path behind the bench allowed direct, quick access.

distractors.1: Several less popular benches actually provided wider views.
distractors.2: Approaching from outside the park was not the preference being explained.
distractors.3: Visitors valued rapid access, not greater separation.

questions.prompt: What implication did the architect draw from the study?
options: Designers should place every bench at the edge of one corner.
Designers should prefer the shortest path even when visibility is poor.
Designers should remove benches from the edges of playgrounds.
Designers should consider both views and how people move from seats.

explanation.correct: The example shows that sitting and moving are related uses that should be designed together.

distractors.0: One bench illustrated the issue; no universal corner rule was proposed.
distractors.1: Caregivers also rejected seating without a usable view.
distractors.2: The improved layouts still include nearby seating.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on evaluating old photographs.
lecture.script: The first photographs in an archive seem to show a city with nearly empty streets. This does not mean the streets were actually quiet. The earliest camera equipment needed time to record enough light. People passing by often moved out of the frame too quickly to leave a clear image. Buildings and parked vehicles remained in place, so those objects are easier to identify.

questions.prompt: What is the lecturer explaining about the early photographs?
options: The photographers deliberately chose streets without traffic.
The equipment made moving people less likely to appear clearly.
The buildings are more visible because they were painted in lighter colors.
Most people stayed indoors while photographs were taken.

explanation.correct: Moving people did not stay visible long enough for the early equipment.

distractors.0: The pictures that look empty may actually have been taken in busy places.
distractors.2: The explanation given is that buildings remained still.
distractors.3: The lecturer questions that inference from a nearly empty image.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on supermarket packaging.
lecture.script: A retailer introduced a clear window into the packaging of a dry food after customers said they disliked buying products they could not see. In a small pilot, customers picked up the packages with the window much more often. Sales, however, barely changed. Researchers then looked at what shoppers did after picking up a package. Many put it down and chose the same brand in a larger size, which was sold in the old packaging. The window appeared to attract attention to the brand, but it did not necessarily persuade people to buy the package they had inspected. Before judging the redesign, the retailer should check whether it increased sales of the brand across all sizes rather than counting only purchases of the one redesigned package.

questions.prompt: Why does the lecturer suggest analyzing sales across package sizes?
options: The two package sizes were available in different stores.
Interest in one package may have led to purchases of a different size.
The window was introduced on both package sizes at the same time.
The researchers were unable to observe what shoppers picked up.

explanation.correct: People sometimes inspected the window package and bought the larger version of the same brand.

distractors.0: Both versions were available to the observed shoppers.
distractors.2: The larger size still used the old packaging.
distractors.3: The researchers observed inspection as well as subsequent purchases.

questions.prompt: What did the pilot show about the packages with windows?
options: Their sales rose sharply.
They were bought mainly by customers seeking a large size.
Shoppers complained that the windows obscured the food.
Shoppers handled them more often than before.

explanation.correct: The window drew people to inspect the package more often.

distractors.0: Sales barely changed.
distractors.1: Shoppers who wanted the larger size often selected a different package.
distractors.2: The initial concern was that the original package concealed the product.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on an experiment with bus schedules.
lecture.script: A regional bus operator wanted to improve service along a route where passengers frequently waited longer than expected. Its first proposal was to add another bus. Before committing to that expense, planners compared the gaps between vehicles arriving at the busiest stops. The timetable promised a bus every twelve minutes, but actual gaps varied widely. A driver arriving a few minutes late found more people waiting and needed longer to board them. The next bus, arriving not long afterward, picked up fewer people and moved faster. Under those conditions two buses sometimes reached the same stop almost together, leaving a much longer gap behind them. The planners tried a holding rule. A bus that was too close to the one ahead waited briefly at a designated point before continuing. This delayed some people already on board, so the operator measured door-to-door journey times as well as waiting times. On average the reduction in long waits outweighed the small delays during the journey. The service became more reliable without another vehicle, though the operator kept the possibility of adding capacity if total demand later rose.

questions.prompt: What caused a following bus to gain on a bus that was already late?
options: It skipped stops where nobody had requested a ride.
It traveled on a shorter route during the experiment.
It collected fewer passengers, so boarding took less time.
It was given priority at all major intersections.

explanation.correct: The late bus accumulated more boarders while the next bus had fewer to pick up.

distractors.0: The buses followed the same stops; skipping is not part of the explanation.
distractors.1: The problem happened between buses on one route.
distractors.3: The lecture discusses boarding time, not signals or priority.

questions.prompt: Why did the operator measure entire journeys as well as time at the stop?
options: The new rule could lengthen the time that some passengers spent on board.
Waiting times were impossible to record accurately.
A change in ticket prices might affect passengers’ choices.
The experiment required some passengers to change vehicles.

explanation.correct: A holding stop could delay people already on the bus, so both effects had to be considered.

distractors.1: The operator had already measured the gaps at the stops.
distractors.2: Ticket prices were not changed or measured in the example.
distractors.3: There was no new change-of-bus requirement.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on library attendance.
lecture.script: A library once reported that its summer exhibits were growing in popularity because the entrance counter recorded more visits. Then staff discovered that some visitors stepped outside to make phone calls and returned through the same doorway. Each return counted as another visit. The figures were still useful for estimating traffic through the door, but they were a poor measure of the number of individuals who attended.

questions.prompt: Why did the library reconsider its claim about attendance?
options: People attending exhibitions normally used a different doorway.
The figures included fewer visits than staff had expected.
The counter could count the same person several times.
The number of exhibitions had increased that summer.

explanation.correct: The device counts entries, and some entries were repeated trips by one visitor.

distractors.0: The returns occurred at the doorway where the device was installed.
distractors.1: Records showed higher entries, but their interpretation was the problem.
distractors.3: No change in the number of exhibits is given as the explanation.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on sound in a renovated hall.
lecture.script: A committee renovating a lecture hall asked an engineer to make speech clearer. The back wall was hard and smooth, and a clap near the stage produced a distinct delayed reflection. The engineer proposed hanging thick fabric over that wall. Before approving it, the committee tried the proposal using temporary curtains. The echo was reduced, but listeners near the rear of the hall said quiet speakers were now harder to hear. The existing sound system could not compensate uniformly because its loudspeakers all faced the front rows. The committee therefore shifted from a one-part solution to a combination: some fabric, plus additional speakers directed toward the rear seats. The trial mattered because fixing a measurable acoustic problem did not by itself guarantee a better listening experience everywhere in the room.

questions.prompt: What unexpected drawback did the temporary curtains reveal?
options: Quiet voices became harder to hear in some seats.
The curtains amplified the echo from the back wall.
Listeners in the front rows heard the speakers too loudly.
The new loudspeakers were too costly to install.

explanation.correct: People toward the rear heard quieter speech less well even though the echo was reduced.

distractors.1: The fabric reduced the delayed reflection.
distractors.2: The complaint came from the rear and concerned insufficient sound.
distractors.3: Additional speakers were part of the eventual plan, not a drawback of the trial.

questions.prompt: Why was the old sound system insufficient for the revised design?
options: It had only temporary fabric coverings.
It produced the distinct reflection studied at the beginning.
Its amplifiers had been removed before the test.
Its speakers were aimed at the front of the room.

explanation.correct: The placement and direction of its speakers limited how evenly they helped listeners.

distractors.0: The curtains were placed on the wall, not over equipment.
distractors.1: The hard wall reflected sound; the loudspeakers did not cause the original reflection.
distractors.2: The old system's direction is identified, not missing amplifiers.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on collecting oral histories.
lecture.script: A historian interviewing retired railway staff often asked everyone to describe a particular strike. At first, she held the interviews in the former station, a building many participants had known throughout their careers. They told detailed stories about station activity but said little about what happened in their homes. Later interviews took place in participants' kitchens because the station was being renovated. Several people suddenly mentioned arranging childcare, sharing food with neighbors, or discussing whether to join the strike with a family member. The historian could have interpreted the later answers as evidence that those interviewees had experienced the strike differently. However, some of these people had already spoken with her at the station and were simply adding memories. She concluded that the setting may cue different parts of a person's experience. To investigate, she invited others to bring a personal object or a work object to an interview, then compared the kinds of stories associated with each. She stresses that neither setting yields a complete account. Each may make some details salient and leave others easier to overlook.

questions.prompt: What evidence suggested that the interview location might influence the answers?
options: The later participants had worked at a different station.
Some of the same people recalled additional domestic details in a new location.
Participants gave less detailed answers after the station closed.
Some stories contradicted dates in official strike records.

explanation.correct: Repeat interviews with some individuals reduce the likelihood that a change of participants fully explains the change.

distractors.0: The passage discusses a shared former station.
distractors.2: The later interviews added memories rather than generally reducing detail.
distractors.3: The issue concerns which details are remembered, not errors against written dates.

questions.prompt: What was the purpose of inviting people to bring an object?
options: To establish which participants had joined the strike.
To explore whether different cues encouraged different kinds of memories.
To collect objects for an exhibition about railway work.
To confirm whether the domestic stories were factually correct.

explanation.correct: The historian compared stories associated with work or personal objects.

distractors.0: Participation in the strike was not the aim of comparing cues.
distractors.2: Objects were brought into interviews, with no plan to collect them.
distractors.3: The comparison tested what prompts memories rather than verifying them independently.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on displaying typeset books.
lecture.script: Printers once kept metal letters in cases divided into compartments. The most frequently needed letters were stored where the printer could reach them easily. The arrangement therefore differed from alphabetical order. A visitor looking only at rows of compartments might assume that some letters were missing. In fact, the order is evidence of working habits, much as the layout of a modern keyboard is.

questions.prompt: What does the arrangement of the old letter cases reveal?
options: Why printers stopped using the alphabet.
Which printers had lost parts of their type.
What size letters a printer could print.
How printers made often-used letters easy to reach.

explanation.correct: Placement depended on frequency and convenience rather than the alphabet.

distractors.0: The order of the cases was different from alphabetical order, but typeset books still used the alphabet.
distractors.1: A visitor may think letters are missing, yet their seeming absence is attributed to layout.
distractors.2: Compartment order is presented as evidence about usage and reach.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on measuring home energy use.
lecture.script: An energy adviser asked residents to read their electricity meters each evening for a month. A household reported one day with extraordinarily low use and attributed it to replacing a kitchen appliance. When staff checked the records, they found that Tuesday's meter reading had been taken shortly after breakfast. Wednesday's was taken at the usual evening hour. The low figure labeled Tuesday therefore covered fewer hours than normal, while the figure labeled Wednesday covered more. Rather than treating one day's number as proof that the appliance saved energy, the adviser combined the two figures and compared electricity use over the full interval. The example shows why the timing of a measurement can matter just as much as the accuracy with which the number is recorded.

questions.prompt: Why did the adviser combine Tuesday's and Wednesday's figures?
options: The meter gave the same reading on both evenings.
The old appliance was used only on Wednesday.
Together they covered the normal span for two days.
Electricity use was higher than expected on both days.

explanation.correct: Adding the periods offsets the shortened Tuesday interval and lengthened Wednesday interval.

distractors.0: Tuesday's reading was made in the morning, not at the standard evening time.
distractors.1: The talk supplies no such comparison between appliances across the two days.
distractors.3: The two daily figures varied in opposite directions because reading times differed.

questions.prompt: What general point is illustrated by the example?
options: An accurate number can mislead when its measurement period is unusual.
Residents usually misread meters after changing an appliance.
Two days of figures are enough to establish annual savings.
New appliances save more electricity early in the day.

explanation.correct: The problem was how much time the number covered, not how accurately it was read.

distractors.1: There is no reported reading error.
distractors.2: The example does not justify projecting savings over a year.
distractors.3: The savings claim was precisely what the timing issue made uncertain.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on evaluating public information campaigns.
lecture.script: A city launched a series of posters encouraging readers to bring books back to the library by their due dates. The staff hoped for a simple measure of success: a decline in the number of overdue books. Over the first month that number did fall, but the change coincided with a reduction in the total number of books borrowed. Even if borrowers behaved exactly as before, fewer loans would usually mean fewer returns occurring late. Staff recalculated the figures as the proportion of all loans that became overdue. This time the change was much smaller. There was another complication. Two elementary schools had paused their regular visits, and books borrowed during school trips were usually brought back together by a teacher. The kind of borrower represented in the figures had also changed. The staff compared loan records within borrower groups and checked whether the remaining groups returned books earlier than comparable groups had before the posters went up. The comparisons could not rule out every outside influence, but they helped separate changes in borrowing patterns from a change in return habits.

questions.prompt: Why might the total number of overdue books fall even if return habits did not change?
options: Teachers returned fewer books together that month.
The library shortened the borrowing period for each book.
There were fewer borrowed books that could become overdue.
The staff changed the definition of an overdue book.

explanation.correct: With fewer total loans, the same rate of late returns yields a lower count.

distractors.0: That concerns borrower composition, while the question asks why the total could drop with the same behavior.
distractors.1: The length of the permitted borrowing period is not said to have changed.
distractors.3: No redefinition of an overdue loan is described.

questions.prompt: What was the purpose of comparing records within borrower groups?
options: To account for a change in who was borrowing books.
To determine how many people had seen the posters.
To explain why the schools stopped visiting.
To identify the books most often returned late.

explanation.correct: People in different groups could have different return habits, so a change in the mix might affect the overall figure.

distractors.1: Loan records did not measure whether a borrower saw an advertisement.
distractors.2: The pause in school visits is treated as a source of bias rather than a finding to explain.
distractors.3: The analysis compared groups of borrowers, not titles.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on making public clocks easier to read.
lecture.script: A municipal clock has a dark face and thin brass hands. On cloudy days the hands stand out. On bright days, a patch of sunlight reflected by the face can make them difficult to see. The maintenance team first considered painting the hands a lighter color, but a trial showed that shading the clock face solved the problem without changing its original materials.

questions.prompt: What did the maintenance team discover in its trial?
options: A lighter paint stopped the brass from reflecting light.
The hands were hard to read on cloudy days.
The clock could be improved only by replacing its face.
Shading the face made the hands easier to see.

explanation.correct: Shade reduced the glare while preserving the original materials.

distractors.0: Painting was considered, but the successful trial used shade.
distractors.1: The hands already stood out on cloudy days.
distractors.2: The trial worked without replacing original components.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on measuring snow in mountains.
lecture.script: A snow gauge near a mountain road can provide a consistent series of measurements at a fixed point. For a water manager, however, that point may represent only a small fraction of the surrounding basin. Wind moves snow across ridges into sheltered hollows, so two sites less than a kilometer apart can have very different depths. An aerial survey can show where the snow lies across a broad area, but a photograph does not reveal exactly how much water the snow contains. To estimate the total more accurately, mountain teams combine aerial maps with samples taken from several kinds of terrain. The maps put each sample into spatial context, and the samples reveal properties the image alone cannot show.

questions.prompt: Why can a single snow gauge give an incomplete picture of the basin?
options: Its records cover too many changes of season.
Nearby sites can hold very different amounts of snow.
It usually measures the deepest hollow in the area.
Its measurements cannot be repeated at one location.

explanation.correct: Wind redistribution means the reading at one spot may be unrepresentative.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on a translation project.
lecture.script: A publisher was preparing an English edition of essays in which one word appeared repeatedly. In some passages it referred to a promise between friends. In others it referred to a public obligation. The translators first chose a different English expression in each setting, trying to make every sentence sound natural. A reader who knew the original then pointed out a consequence. The essays revisit the same word to encourage readers to notice a connection between private promises and public obligations. Because the English phrases differed, the pattern was difficult to detect. Simply using one English word everywhere would retain the repetition but could sound strange or misleading in some passages. The team decided to use a recurring English expression in passages where the connection mattered most, adjusting the nearby wording so it made sense. Elsewhere, it used a more natural local equivalent and explained the choice in an introduction. The project illustrates why a translator may need to make a decision at the level of a whole book, as well as at the level of individual sentences.

options: A repeated English expression sounded unnatural throughout the book.

explanation.correct: Different local translations hid a pattern spanning the essays.

distractors.0: Reusing exactly one translation was discussed later as a different approach.
distractors.1: The initial translations preserved local meanings; the relationship between them was harder to notice.
distractors.2: The introduction was part of the later compromise, not a consequence of the initial choices.

questions.prompt: How did the team make a repeated English expression work in selected passages?

It adapted the surrounding wording.
It put the original word beside each English phrase.

explanation.correct: The team adjusted nearby language so the recurring choice remained natural.

distractors.0: The essays retained their separate contexts.
distractors.1: The link between private and public obligations was important to preserve.
distractors.3: The talk mentions an introduction rather than parallel text beside each phrase.

The manager collected occupancy figures and reported water use per resident as well. That made the comparison more meaningful, although the figures still could not distinguish indoor consumption from watering a shared garden. She therefore treated the new calculation as an improvement in the measure rather than a complete explanation of how the water was used.

lecture.context: Listen to part of a lecture on reconstructing local history from advertisements.
lecture.script: A historian studying a town's bakeries kept finding the phrase freshly baked in its old newspapers. She initially treated each advertisement as evidence that a shop was producing bread on its premises. Then she noticed that several shops used precisely the same illustration and wording. The similarity did not by itself show those shops lacked ovens. A printing company could have supplied a shared design to independent businesses. However, the historian obtained delivery books from one bakery and found that it supplied bread every morning to several of the advertising shops. The publicity therefore recorded where fresh bread was sold, but at least some notices did not identify where it had been baked. To extend her study, the historian compared advertisements with building plans that showed ovens and with leases that gave tenants permission to bake. These sources also had limits. An oven installed in a building might not be used, and permission does not establish that a tenant exercised it. By comparing sources, she developed a map that marked firm identifications separately from plausible ones. Her goal was to make the degree of uncertainty visible.

continuation.script: Three letters from the same week describe empty shops in the town center. All three were addressed to one supplier and asked for more deliveries. A historian should consider whether the writers emphasized shortages because they wanted to

questions.prompt: Choose the words that best complete the recording about the letters.
options: keep suppliers out of the town center
persuade the supplier to send goods
explain why demand had already collapsed
prevent the supplier from learning about shortages

explanation.correct: Requests for more deliveries give the authors a motive to stress the shortage.

distractors.0: The letters invite more supply rather than asking the recipient to stay away.
distractors.2: A shortage does not establish collapsing demand.
distractors.3: The authors explicitly discussed empty shops and did not try to conceal them.

continuation.context: Listen to part of a lecture on comparing microscope images.
continuation.script: The first microscope image showed several grains with sharp edges. In the second image, taken at a lower magnification, the edges looked smooth. Before concluding that the grains themselves had changed, a researcher should photograph them

questions.prompt: Choose the words that best complete the recording about the images.
options: at an even lower magnification
with their edges removed
only after changing their composition
under comparable viewing conditions

explanation.correct: A comparison should control the imaging conditions before attributing an appearance change to the object.

distractors.0: Further lowering magnification preserves rather than resolves the mismatch.
distractors.1: Removing edges would change what the researcher wants to compare.
distractors.2: Changing the composition would create exactly the physical difference under investigation.
